name: Dokku
summary: A Heroku-like PaaS on one server of your own: `git push` to it, and Dokku builds the app with buildpacks or a Dockerfile and runs it in Docker containers behind nginx.
intro: Dokku installs on a single Ubuntu or Debian machine with at least 1 GB of memory. You create an app on the host (`dokku apps:create`), add a Git remote such as `dokku@dokku.me:ruby-getting-started` and `git push` to it over SSH. A builder turns the code into an image: by default `herokuish`, which runs Heroku’s classic buildpacks; `pack`, which runs Cloud Native Buildpacks; or `dockerfile` when the repository only has a Dockerfile. Prebuilt Docker images work too. The default scheduler then starts the processes from your `Procfile` as containers on the local Docker daemon, nginx routes each app’s domain to its `web` containers, and Dokku manages cron tasks and background processes as well.

Almost everything is a plugin: Dokku itself is a collection of plugins run by `plugn`. Datastores aren’t built in. Official plugins such as `dokku-postgres` create a database container, and `dokku postgres:link` sets `DATABASE_URL` on the app, the same contract as a Heroku add-on. Deploys are zero-downtime by default: Dokku waits 10 seconds after starting each new container (or runs your checks), switches traffic, then sends `SIGTERM` to the old containers. For more than one server, the K3s scheduler (since 0.33.0) runs apps on a Dokku-managed K3s cluster, with KEDA for autoscaling.
strengths: A Heroku-style workflow (`git push`, `Procfile`, buildpacks, config as env vars) on a single VM you already pay for
Three builders and plain Docker images, so the same host runs buildpack apps and Dockerfile apps side by side
Official plugins for common datastores, plus community plugins, all wired up through environment variables
MIT-licensed and actively released: v0.38.31 shipped in September 2026
limits: By default everything, apps and databases included, runs on one host, so that host is a single point of failure and its OS, Docker and backups are yours to run
Multi-server setups mean the K3s scheduler, which needs at least 2 GB of memory on every node and brings Kubernetes with it
Apps must listen on the port in `$PORT`, or they won’t answer web requests
Still versioned 0.x after more than 13 years, so read the upgrade notes before each release

snippet.title: Deploy a Rails app with a Postgres database
source: dokku postgres:link railsdatabase ruby-getting-started   # sets DATABASE_URL
git push dokku main      # herokuish build, then a zero-downtime deploy
# back on the host: two web containers behind nginx

story: Jeff Lindsay made the first Dokku commit on June 8, 2013. The README called it a “Docker powered mini-Heroku” and “the smallest PaaS implementation you’ve ever seen”. It glued together three small projects: Docker to run containers, Buildstep to build apps with Heroku buildpacks (Node.js and Ruby at first), and gitreceive to accept a `git push`.

The point was size and speed. The first README said installing took around 5 minutes, “certainly better than the several hours it takes to bootstrap Cloud Foundry”. The first outside pull request, a day later, prepared it for Java apps. Over the following years Dokku grew a plugin system, official datastore plugins and a choice of builders, including Cloud Native Buildpacks.

Dokku stayed a single-server tool by default, but builders (0.24.0, 2021) and schedulers (0.26.0, 2021) became pluggable, and in 2024 version 0.33.0 added a K3s scheduler that spreads apps over a cluster of servers while keeping the same `git push` workflow.

choices.choice: Assemble existing tools instead of building a platform
choices.why: The first version was Docker, a buildpack runner and a Git receiver wired together by a bootstrap script, and it installed in about 5 minutes instead of the hours a full platform such as Cloud Foundry took.
Using Heroku’s buildpacks and `Procfile` meant apps written for Heroku, such as Heroku’s own getting-started apps, deploy to Dokku unchanged.
Dokku’s own features are plugins run by `plugn`, so datastores, builders and schedulers can be added or swapped without changing the core.

timeline.text: Jeff Lindsay makes the first commit on June 8: Docker, Buildstep and gitreceive
Pluggable builders arrive in 0.24.0 (March) and schedulers in 0.26.0 (October)
0.33.0 adds the K3s scheduler for multi-server clusters (January)
